book.title: Mahmud Kashgari and His Work Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk

pages.title: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
pages.content:
In this text, you will learn about the world’s oldest Turkish dictionary and its author. The name of this dictionary is Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk. It means ‘Dictionary of Turkish Languages’. Today, people can find the only copy of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk in Istanbul, at the Millet Library.

Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is a historical dictionary from the 11th century by Mahmud Kashgari. He wrote it to teach Turkish to Arabs. He also wanted to show everyone that Turkish is a rich language, beautiful to write and speak. In 1072, Mahmud of Kashgar started writing his great book. He made new additions many times and finished it in 1074. Later, in 1077, he presented his work to the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad.

Today modern Turkish has 132,334 words. This dictionary from the 11th century has about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms, though. You can see the oldest Turkish poems and learn grammar rules of the Turkish language. The book lists many place names and personal names. It shares old traditions with interesting legends from the Turkic world. This book describes daily life then, so it is a big guide to Turkish culture.

In addition to all the language notes, it has a map of the old Turkic world. Because of this map, Kashgari became the very first Turkic mapmaker in history. The map shows where the Turks lived and the nations they met. On it, mountains are marked in red, seas in green, rivers in blue, and sandy areas in yellow. The map in Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is very important because it is the first world map to show Japan. The second world map with Japan was made 400 years later.

pages.title: Who Was Mahmud Kashgari?
pages.content: Historians believe that Mahmud Kashgari was born in Barsgan, Kyrgyzstan, in 1008 and died in Kashgar in 1105. Kashgar is a very old city in western China. It is known as an ancient Turkic homeland and is also called East Turkestan. Mahmud Kashgari came from a noble Karakhanid family. In his book, he describes himself like this: “I am a very smart person from an important family. I speak Turkish perfectly, express my ideas clearly, and I am great at throwing spears.”

pages.title: In Praise of the Turks and Their Language
pages.content:
In his book, he says that Allah gave the name ‘Turk’ to the Turkish people. He adds that Allah gave the Turks this name and put them in the highest and cleanest part of the world. He writes that Allah called them ‘My army.’ He also says that the Turks have many great qualities. They are beautiful, polite, respectful to older people, honest, and brave. He also shares this hadith. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) says, “Learn the Turkish language! Because the Turks will rule for a very long time.” With a deep belief in his heart, Mahmud of Kashgar began his journey in 1057 to visit every Turkic land. For about ten to fifteen years, he traveled from tribe to tribe, learned their unique dialects, and gathered valuable stories and notes before finally reaching the great city of Baghdad.

In Karakhanid schools, Arabic was the main language for teaching and writing. This made Mahmud Kashgari want to praise his native language, Turkish. He believed Turkish was just as great as Arabic. To prove this, he wrote the famous book Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk.

vocabulary.definition: Good parts of a person’s character.

pages.title: The Story of the Calendar
pages.content:
In this old dictionary, we find an interesting calendar. Turkish people have used it since ancient times. Kashgari describes this calendar as the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar. He explains how it started and its role in the lives of the Turks. He writes that the Turks created a 12-year calendar with 12 different animals. This special calendar helped them keep track of their children’s ages, battle dates, and other big moments. Here is the interesting story of this calendar:

A long time ago, a Turkic khan (a title Turkish rulers used long before Islam) wanted to learn about a battle from the past. But his people disagreed about the date, so the khan called a great kurultay to ask them. A Kurultay was a national meeting or general meeting at that time.

The khan said: “If we are wrong about this date, the people after us will also be wrong. To stop this, let’s make a calendar with the twelve stars of the sky and the twelve months, and give a name to each year. In this way, we will find the time by counting these years. This system should be a record for all of us.”

The people loved the khan’s idea too, and they named the years in this way:

The khan went to hunt. He told the people to push the wild animals toward a big river in the Ili Valley. The people chased the animals to the water. The river was dangerous, so only twelve animals could cross to the other side safely. The Turkish calendar started with the Year of the Rat because the rat crossed the river first. After that, each new year got its name from the other animals in the order they crossed.

pages.title: The Twelve Animals
pages.content:
This is the list of the animals:

1. Year of the Sıçgan means ‘Year of the Rat’

2. Year of the Ud means ‘Year of the Ox’

3. Year of the Bars means ‘Year of the Leopard’

4. Year of the Tavışgan means ‘Year of the Rabbit’

5. Year of the Nag means ‘Year of the Crocodile’

6. Year of the Yılan means ‘Year of the Snake’

7. Year of the Yund means ‘Year of the Horse’

8. Year of the Koy means ‘Year of the Sheep’

9. Year of the Biçin means ‘Year of the Monkey’

10. Year of the Takagu means ‘Year of the Rooster’

11. Year of the İt means ‘Year of the Dog’

12. Year of the Toŋguz means ‘Year of the Pig’

pages.title: What Each Year Means
pages.content:
According to very old Turkish beliefs, every year has a special meaning. For example, people believe that more wars will happen in the Year of the Ox, because the ox is an animal that likes to fight with its horns. The Year of the Rooster brings plenty of food, but it also brings a lot of trouble. This is because roosters eat grain and love to dig in the garbage. When the Year of the Snake and the Year of the Crocodile start, rain and growth come because these animals naturally live in or near water. When the Year of the Pig starts, snow gets worse and trouble grows. In this way, people give different meanings to each new year.

Once the Year of the Pig ends, the calendar goes back to the beginning with the Year of the Rat. This calendar says the Earth is 3.6 million years old. One cycle lasts 12 years. A year has 12 months, 365 days, and about 5 hours. The 7 days of the week do not have any names. A new day starts at midnight and is divided into 12 equal parts. So, each part lasts for two hours.

According to Kashgari, the old Turkish calendar started on March 21st. Turks celebrated this day as the beginning of the new year in many places from Central Asia to the Middle East and the Balkans. They called it Nowruz. It means “new day.”

pages.title: The First World Map with Japan
pages.content:
In addition to all this information, there is also a world map in the book. Because of this map, people know Kashgari as the first Turkic mapmaker.

Mahmud of Kashgar said that Allah put the Turks on the highest mountains, the center of the world, so they could rule the earth and control the whole world. On the map, Turkestan, the home of the Turks, is in the middle of the world. The city of Balasagun in Kyrgyzstan is right in the heart of this Turkic land. Balasagun was on a very busy part of the Silk Road. He drew all other countries, cities, and mountains around this place. The map has a colorful, round design. It shows mountains in red, seas in green, rivers in blue, and sandy areas in yellow.

According to modern maps, Mahmud of Kashgar’s world map goes as far west as Russia and the Idil (Volga) River. In the south, the map shows the area from Egypt to Ethiopia and India. In the east, it shows China and Japan. On the map, Japan has the name ‘Jabarqa’ and China is called ‘the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc.’

With our information today, the map in Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first world map to show Japan. The second map to show Japan was made four hundred years after his book.

pages.title: A Treasure of the Turkish Language
pages.content:
Mahmud of Kashgar is a very important person for the Turkish language. His book is the biggest treasure of the Turkish language. At Turkey’s suggestion, UNESCO included his famous book, Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, in its 2024 celebration program. Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan also worked together on it.

This great book still waits for new students to learn more secrets about our history.

His book is the [choice] treasure of the Turkish language.
Mahmud of Kashgar is a very [choice] person for the Turkish language.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Use “the + -est” to compare one thing with all the others. Use “very + adjective” without comparing.

feedback.incorrect: Is the sentence comparing with all the others?

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: A Treasure of My Culture
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tell your partner about a treasure of your culture.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is it? Why is it important?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “A treasure of my culture is the Mevlana Museum in Konya. It is the most beautiful building in my town. It is important because many people visit it and learn about our history.”

discussionPrompts.question: Say what the treasure is.
discussionPrompts.example: A treasure of my culture is …

discussionPrompts.question: Use the + -est.
discussionPrompts.example: It is the oldest / most beautiful …

discussionPrompts.question: Say why it is important.

beforeYouRead.question: Guess first: Which year did UNESCO celebrate the book?

iCan: I can say why Kashgari’s book is a treasure.
I can name countries that worked together for the book.
I can use the biggest and very important.

groupTask.title: Our Twelve-Animal Calendar Poster
steps: Draw a big circle and divide it into twelve parts.
Write the twelve animals in order with their old Turkic names.
Add one sentence from the book about the calendar or Nowruz.
Present your poster and say why Kashgari’s book is a treasure.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its poster. The class finds the first and the last animal on every poster.
groupTask.solo: Make a small calendar card with your birth year’s animal and two sentences from the book.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your understanding of the complete book.

exercises.title: What Is It?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: What is Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk?
options: a historical dictionary from the 11th century
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is a historical dictionary from the 11th century by Mahmud Kashgari.”

feedback.correct: Correct. A historical dictionary from the 11th century.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 1.

exercises.title: How Many Words?
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: The dictionary has about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs and idioms.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “This dictionary from the 11th century has about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms, though.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the third paragraph of Chapter 1.

exercises.title: Where Was He Born?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: Where was Mahmud Kashgari born?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “Mahmud Kashgari was born in Barsgan, Kyrgyzstan, in 1008 …”

feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentence of Chapter 2.

exercises.title: The Journey
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: Kashgari began his journey to visit every Turkic land in 1057.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “Mahmud of Kashgar began his journey in 1057 to visit every Turkic land.”

feedback.incorrect: Find the word journey in Chapter 3.

exercises.title: The Calendar
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: What did the calendar help the Turks keep track of?
options: their children’s ages and battle dates
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “This special calendar helped them keep track of their children’s ages, battle dates, and other big moments.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 4.

exercises.title: The First Year
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: The calendar started with the Year of the Horse.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “The Turkish calendar started with the Year of the Rat because the rat crossed the river first.”

feedback.correct: Correct. It started with the Year of the Rat.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 4.

exercises.title: The New Year
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: When did the old Turkish calendar start?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “According to Kashgari, the old Turkish calendar started on March 21st.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 6.

exercises.title: The Map
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: Why is the map in the book very important?
options: It is the first world map to show Japan.
It is the biggest map in the world.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “With our information today, the map in Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first world map to show Japan.”

feedback.correct: Correct. It is the first world map to show Japan.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 7.

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the book in one place.

vocabulary.definition: Most old; from the earliest time.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: In this text, you will learn about the world’s oldest Turkish dictionary and its author.

vocabulary.definition: The person who wrote a book.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: In this text, you will learn about the world’s oldest Turkish dictionary and its author.

vocabulary.definition: The meaning of the name Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: It means ‘Dictionary of Turkish Languages’.

vocabulary.definition: Used to show that something is surprising.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: This dictionary from the 11th century has about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms, though.

vocabulary.definition: Very old stories, often not all true.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: It shares old traditions with interesting legends from the Turkic world.

vocabulary.definition: Tells what something is like.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: This book describes daily life then, so it is a big guide to Turkish culture.

vocabulary.definition: Something that helps you understand or find your way.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Oldest Dictionary of the Turkic World
vocabulary.storyExample: This book describes daily life then, so it is a big guide to Turkish culture.

vocabulary.definition: An old city in western China.
vocabulary.storyExample: Historians believe that Mahmud Kashgari was born in Barsgan, Kyrgyzstan, in 1008 and died in Kashgar in 1105.

vocabulary.definition: An old Turkic homeland in western China.
vocabulary.storyExample: It is known as an ancient Turkic homeland and is also called East Turkestan.

vocabulary.definition: With no mistakes.
vocabulary.storyExample: I speak Turkish perfectly, express my ideas clearly, and I am great at throwing spears.”

vocabulary.definition: Sending long, sharp sticks through the air.
vocabulary.storyExample: I speak Turkish perfectly, express my ideas clearly, and I am great at throwing spears.”

vocabulary.definition: Good parts of a person’s character.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: In Praise of the Turks and Their Language
vocabulary.storyExample: He writes that Allah called them ‘My army.’ He also says that the Turks have many great qualities.

vocabulary.definition: From very old (times) until now.
vocabulary.storyExample: Turkish people have used it since ancient times.

vocabulary.definition: Remember or record something so you do not forget it.
vocabulary.storyExample: This special calendar helped them keep track of their children’s ages, battle dates, and other big moments.

vocabulary.definition: Had different ideas.
vocabulary.storyExample: But his people disagreed about the date, so the khan called a great kurultay to ask them.

vocabulary.definition: A big national meeting of the Turks.
vocabulary.storyExample: But his people disagreed about the date, so the khan called a great kurultay to ask them.

vocabulary.definition: Animals that do not live with people.
vocabulary.storyExample: He told the people to push the wild animals toward a big river in the Ili Valley.

vocabulary.definition: A valley with a big river in Central Asia.
vocabulary.storyExample: He told the people to push the wild animals toward a big river in the Ili Valley.

vocabulary.definition: Go from one side to the other.
vocabulary.storyExample: The river was dangerous, so only twelve animals could cross to the other side safely.

vocabulary.definition: Without danger.
vocabulary.storyExample: The river was dangerous, so only twelve animals could cross to the other side safely.

vocabulary.definition: A small animal like a big mouse.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Turkish calendar started with the Year of the Rat because the rat crossed the river first.

vocabulary.definition: A big, strong male cow.
vocabulary.storyExample: Year of the Ud means ‘Year of the Ox’ 3.

vocabulary.definition: A big animal with a long mouth that lives in rivers.
vocabulary.storyExample: Year of the Nag means ‘Year of the Crocodile’ 6.

vocabulary.definition: A male chicken.
vocabulary.storyExample: Year of the Takagu means ‘Year of the Rooster’ 11.

vocabulary.definition: Hard, pointed parts on the head of some animals.
vocabulary.storyExample: For example, people believe that more wars will happen in the Year of the Ox, because the ox is an animal that likes to fight with its horns.

vocabulary.definition: Problems and difficulties.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Year of the Rooster brings plenty of food, but it also brings a lot of trouble.

vocabulary.definition: Continues for a time.
vocabulary.storyExample: One cycle lasts 12 years.

vocabulary.definition: Had a happy event for a special day.
vocabulary.storyExample: Turks celebrated this day as the beginning of the new year in many places from Central Asia to the Middle East and the Balkans.

vocabulary.definition: The old Turkish New Year on March 21st.
vocabulary.storyExample: They called it Nowruz.

vocabulary.definition: Old trade roads between China and the West.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The First World Map with Japan
vocabulary.storyExample: Balasagun was on a very busy part of the Silk Road.

vocabulary.definition: The name for China on Kashgari’s map.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The First World Map with Japan
vocabulary.storyExample: On the map, Japan has the name ‘Jabarqa’ and China is called ‘the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc.’ With our information today, the map in Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first world map to show Japan.

vocabulary.definition: An idea that you give to someone.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: A Treasure of the Turkish Language
vocabulary.storyExample: At Turkey’s suggestion, UNESCO included his famous book, Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, in its 2024 celebration program.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the language of the whole book.

exercises.title: Look: The Book or the Map?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences into two groups.
exercises.question: Is it about the words or about the map?
exercises.explanation: Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is a dictionary, and it also has a world map (Chapters 1 and 7).

feedback.correct: Good. You sorted the words and the map.
feedback.incorrect: Is the sentence about language or about places?

exercises.title: Look: Past Forms
exercises.instructions: Choose the sentence with a correct past form.
exercises.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: Kashgari drew all other countries around this place.
Kashgari drawed all other countries around this place.
Kashgari draw all other countries around this place.
exercises.explanation: “Draw” is an irregular verb. Its past form is “drew”.

feedback.incorrect: What is the past of draw?

exercises.title: Look: To + Verb
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: In “He wrote it to teach Turkish to Arabs”, “to teach” shows why he wrote it.
exercises.explanation: “To + verb” can show a purpose: why someone does something.

feedback.incorrect: Why did he write it?

exercises.title: Practise: Linking Words
exercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word fits?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Arabic was the main language in schools, [blank] Kashgari wanted to praise Turkish. The calendar started with the rat [blank] it crossed first. The Year of the Rooster brings food, [blank] it also brings trouble.
exercises.explanation: “So” gives a result. “Because” gives a reason. “But” shows something different.

feedback.incorrect: Is it a result, a reason or something different?

exercises.title: Practise: Choose the Form
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence.
exercises.question: Which form fits?

formChoices.sentence: The Year of the Ox is the [choice] year.
His book is the [choice] treasure of the Turkish language.

exercises.explanation: Use “in” with years, ordinal numbers for order and “the + -est” to compare with all the others.

feedback.incorrect: Check the preposition, the ordinal and the superlative.

exercises.title: Practise: Correct the Sentences
exercises.instructions: Find the mistake and choose the correct form.
exercises.question: Which form is correct?

errorItems.sentence: The rat crossed the river firstly.
The khan said, “Let’s to make a calendar.”

exercises.explanation: Begin → began. We say “crossed first”. After “let’s”, use the base verb.

feedback.incorrect: Check the irregular verb, the order word and let’s.

exercises.title: Use: A New Context
exercises.instructions: Read about a school library. Fill each gap from the word bank.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words in a new text?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Our school has a small library. The [blank] book in it is from 1950. The [blank] of the book was a teacher. It has many old [blank] from our town. Every year, we [blank] Library Day.
exercises.explanation: Oldest, author, legends and celebrate come from the book. Here they describe a school library.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s words in a new text.
feedback.incorrect: Read the words around each gap.

exercises.title: Use: Check a Short Text
exercises.instructions: A student wrote about a trip. Find each mistake.
exercises.question: What should the student change?

errorItems.sentence: Last summer, we go to Istanbul.
We visited the Millet Library for see the old book.

exercises.explanation: Use “in” with years, a past verb for last summer and “to + verb” for a purpose.

feedback.incorrect: Check the preposition, the verb and the purpose.

exercises.title: Use: Words in My Family
exercises.instructions: Write four to five sentences about old words in your family.
exercises.question: Which old words do older people use?
exercises.explanation: Example: “My grandmother uses the word ‘kuşluk’. It means ‘the middle of the morning’. She learned it from her mother. Today, young people do not use it much. It is good to write old words down because people can forget them.”

feedback.correct: Check: the word, its meaning and because.

discussionPrompts.question: Say who uses the old word.
Say what the word means.
Say why it is good to write old words down, with because.
discussionPrompts.example: It is good to write them down because …

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Bring the whole book together in the Final Challenge.

exercises.title: The Only Copy
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: Where is the only copy of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk today?
options: in Istanbul, at the Millet Library
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Today, people can find the only copy of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk in Istanbul, at the Millet Library.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of the book.

exercises.title: Words and Meanings
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning.
exercises.question: What do the words mean?

matchingPairs.right: the person who wrote a book
an idea that you give to someone

correctAnswer.author: the person who wrote a book
correctAnswer.suggestion: an idea that you give to someone

exercises.explanation: These words are important in the book.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each word matches its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Think about Chapters 1, 4 and 8.

exercises.title: Years
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 1 with one number.
exercises.question: When did Kashgari present his work in Baghdad?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Later, in [blank], he presented his work to the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Later, in 1077, he presented his work to the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 1.

exercises.title: In Praise of Turkish
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: What did Kashgari believe about Turkish?
options: It was just as great as Arabic.
It was not a rich language.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “He believed Turkish was just as great as Arabic.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Just as great as Arabic.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 3.

exercises.title: Years and Meanings
exercises.instructions: Match each year with what it brings in the old beliefs.
exercises.question: What does each year bring?

matchingPairs.right: plenty of food and a lot of trouble

correctAnswer.the Year of the Rooster: plenty of food and a lot of trouble

exercises.explanation: Chapter 6 tells what each year means in the old Turkish beliefs.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each year matches its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 6.

exercises.title: A Day
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: In the calendar, a new day starts at midnight.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “A new day starts at midnight and is divided into 12 equal parts.”

feedback.correct: Correct. A new day starts at midnight.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 6.

exercises.title: The Silk Road
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: Balasagun was far from the Silk Road.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “Balasagun was on a very busy part of the Silk Road.”

feedback.correct: Correct. It was on a very busy part of the Silk Road.
feedback.incorrect: Find the Silk Road in Chapter 7.

exercises.title: Nowruz
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 6 with two words.
exercises.question: What does Nowruz mean?
exercises.fillBlanksText: They called it Nowruz. It means “[blank].”
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “They called it Nowruz. It means ‘new day.’”

feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 6.

exercises.title: Working Together
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer from the book.
exercises.question: Whose suggestion was the UNESCO celebration?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “At Turkey’s suggestion, UNESCO included his famous book …”

feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 8.

exercises.title: The Story of the Book
exercises.instructions: Put the events in order.
exercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: Mahmud Kashgari was born in Barsgan.
Mahmud Kashgari began his journey to every Turkic land.
Mahmud Kashgari started writing his great book.
Mahmud Kashgari presented his work in Baghdad.
UNESCO included the book in its 2024 program.

exercises.explanation: Born in 1008, journey in 1057, writing in 1072, Baghdad in 1077, UNESCO in 2024.

feedback.correct: Correct. From his birth to UNESCO.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the years in Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 8.
